lead: A subgroup H sits inside a group G. Fix an element a and multiply every element of H by a; the result aH is a left coset. Cosets are equal-sized blocks that split G without overlap. Lagrange's theorem states that for a finite group, |H| divides |G|. This one counting fact controls possible subgroup sizes and element orders. It is used in modular arithmetic, cryptography, error-correcting codes and in proving that groups of prime order are cyclic.
prereq: You need groups and subgroups and cyclic groups; equivalence classes from Unit 2 are the model for the partition proof.

sections.h3: Left cosets, right cosets and index

blocks.text: Let (G, ·) be a group with identity e, and let H ≤ G be a subgroup. For a ∈ G, the left coset of H by a is aH = {a h : h ∈ H}. The right coset is Ha = {h a : h ∈ H}. In an abelian group the two are equal. In Z₈ under addition, take H = {0,4}. The left cosets are 0+H = {0,4}, 1+H = {1,5}, 2+H = {2,6}, 3+H = {3,7}. The coset 4+H equals {4,0}, which is 0+H, so it is not new.

The index of H in G, written [G:H], is the number of distinct left cosets. Here [Z₈:H] = 4. Every a lies in its own coset aH because e ∈ H. The coset aH is a subgroup exactly when a ∈ H; otherwise it does not contain e. For example, 1+H = {1,5} is not a subgroup of Z₈.

blocks.where: aH and bH are left cosets of H in G; a,b ∈ G; a⁻¹ is the inverse of a; e is the identity.

blocks.text: Define a relation on G by a ~ b when a⁻¹b ∈ H. This is an equivalence relation. Reflexive: a⁻¹a = e ∈ H. Symmetric: if a⁻¹b ∈ H, then (a⁻¹b)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a ∈ H. Transitive: if a⁻¹b ∈ H and b⁻¹c ∈ H, then a⁻¹c = (a⁻¹b)(b⁻¹c) ∈ H, because H is closed. The equivalence class of a is {b : a⁻¹b ∈ H}. The condition a⁻¹b ∈ H is the same as b = a h for some h ∈ H, so the class is exactly aH.

Two cosets are either identical or disjoint. If c ∈ aH ∩ bH, then c = a h₁ = b h₂ for some h₁,h₂ ∈ H. So a⁻¹b = h₁ h₂⁻¹ ∈ H, and the equality test gives aH = bH. Therefore the distinct left cosets form a partition of G.

The map h ↦ a h is a bijection from H to aH. Its inverse is x ↦ a⁻¹x. Hence every coset has the same size as H: |aH| = |H|. This holds for finite groups as an equality of counts. The same proof works for right cosets.

blocks.where: G is a finite group, H ≤ G, [G:H] is the index, |H| is the number of elements in H.

blocks.text: Proof: the distinct left cosets partition G. If there are k = [G:H] cosets and each has |H| elements, then |G| = k |H|. Thus |H| divides |G|. For Z₈ and H={0,4}, |G|=8, |H|=2 and [G:H]=4, so 8 = 4·2.

For any g ∈ G, the subgroup ⟨g⟩ generated by g has order equal to the order of g. Here ord(g), the order of g, is the smallest positive integer n with gⁿ = e (written n·g = 0 in additive notation). By Lagrange, ord(g) divides |G|. So g^{|G|} = e. In additive notation, |G|·g = 0. Example: in Z₈, ord(2)=4 and ord(3)=8; both divide 8.

If |G| = p is prime, any nonidentity g has a subgroup ⟨g⟩ whose order is greater than 1 and divides p. The only possibility is p, so ⟨g⟩ = G and G is cyclic. In the symmetric group S₃ on {1,2,3}, |S₃|=6. For H={e,(12)}, |H|=2, so any left coset has 2 elements and the index is 3. One left coset is (13)H = {(13),(123)}. The right coset H(13) = {(13),(132)} is different, so aH need not equal Ha.

examples.question: In G = Z₈ under addition modulo 8, let H = {0,4}. (a) List all distinct left cosets of H. (b) State the index [G:H]. (c) Verify Lagrange's theorem numerically.
steps: For each a ∈ G compute a+H = {(a+h) mod 8 : h ∈ H}.
For a=4: 4+H = {4,0} = 0+H. For a=5: 5+H = {5,1} = 1+H. For a=6: 6+H = {6,2} = 2+H. For a=7: 7+H = {7,3} = 3+H. So only four cosets are distinct.
examples.answer: The distinct left cosets are {0,4}, {1,5}, {2,6}, {3,7}; [G:H]=4; 8=4×2 verifies Lagrange's theorem.

traps: aH = Ha is not automatic. It holds for every a exactly when H is normal. In S₃ with H={e,(12)}, (13)H ≠ H(13).
A coset is not usually a subgroup. aH contains e only when a ∈ H; otherwise it is just a translate of H.
Use the correct equality test: aH=bH iff a⁻¹b∈H, while Ha=Hb iff ab⁻¹∈H. Mixing the inverse order is a common error.
Lagrange says |H| divides |G| for a subgroup H. The converse is false: a divisor of |G| need not be the order of a subgroup. Also, Lagrange applies only to finite groups.
Do not count repeated cosets: [G:H] is the number of distinct cosets, not |G|.

quiz.q: Define the left coset aH and the index [G:H].
quiz.a: aH={ah:h∈H}; [G:H] is the number of distinct left cosets of H in G.

quiz.q: Why are two left cosets of H either equal or disjoint?
quiz.a: If aH∩bH contains c, then c=ah₁=bh₂, so a⁻¹b=h₁h₂⁻¹∈H; the equality test gives aH=bH.

quiz.q: In G=Z₁₂ under addition, H={0,4,8}. List all distinct left cosets and find [G:H].
In S₃, H={e,(12)}. Find (13)H and H(13). Use composition right-to-left.
A group G has order 15. Can it have a subgroup of order 6? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Lagrange would require 6 divides 15, which is false.

quiz.q: Let G be a group of order 13. Prove G is cyclic.
quiz.a: Take g≠e. |⟨g⟩| divides 13. It is greater than 1, so it is 13. Thus ⟨g⟩=G.

quiz.q: State Lagrange's theorem and one corollary about element order.
quiz.a: For finite G and H≤G, |H| divides |G|. For g∈G, ord(g) divides |G|.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cosets become quotient groups when H is normal; that construction is the gateway to group homomorphisms and exact sequences. In coding theory, cosets of a linear code are used to build syndrome decoding tables. In cryptography, Lagrange's theorem bounds the orders of elements in groups such as Zₚ*, which underpins Diffie–Hellman and RSA-style arithmetic. Search next for 'quotient group', 'group action' and 'coset decoding'.
